subject: Reasoning
topic: Statement: Cause and Effect — Identifying Causal Relationships and Independent Events (W13 B1)

questions.stem: Two statements: (I) The municipal corporation has closed several schools in the old part of the city for safety reasons. (II) Many buildings in the old part of the city have been declared structurally unsafe. Which of these is cause and which is effect?

options.option_text: I is the cause; II is the effect
II is the cause; I is the effect
Both I and II are independent causes of some other effect
Both I and II are effects of some common cause

questions.explanation: B is correct. The logical sequence: Buildings declared structurally unsafe (Statement II) → Corporation closes schools for safety (Statement I). An unsafe building creates a safety concern that CAUSES authorities to take action (closing schools). II is the cause; I is the effect. Trap: I→II would mean closing schools made buildings unsafe (illogical — school closures don't affect building structure).

questions.stem: Two statements: (I) The price of vegetables has risen sharply this season. (II) The state government has announced a relief package for vegetable farmers. Which is cause and which is effect?

options.option_text: I is the cause; II is the effect
II is the cause; I is the effect
Both are independent effects
II is cause and I is also cause

questions.explanation: A is correct. Sharp rise in vegetable prices (I) indicates market distress → government announces relief for farmers (II) in response. Price rise CAUSES the government to act. I is cause; II is effect. Trap: II→I = government relief raising prices is also possible (subsidies can reduce prices, not raise them — so II causing I would mean the relief package RAISED prices, which is counterintuitive).

questions.stem: Two statements: (I) There was a huge traffic jam on the main highway this morning. (II) A new shopping mall opened near the highway this week. Which is cause and which is effect?

options.option_text: I is cause; II is effect
II is cause; I is effect
Both are independent
Both are effects of the same cause

questions.explanation: B is correct. New mall opening (II) attracted increased traffic → traffic jam (I) resulted. A new shopping destination brings additional vehicles to the area. II is cause; I is effect. Trap: I→II = traffic jams don't cause malls to open (illogical — malls cause traffic, not the reverse); 'both independent' = ignores the clear temporal and logical connection (mall opened this week, jam happened this morning).

questions.stem: Two statements: (I) The number of road accidents in the city has increased significantly over the past year. (II) The state has increased the penalty for drunk driving. Which is cause and which is effect?

options.option_text: I is cause; II is effect
II is cause; I is effect
Both are independent
Both are effects of a third cause

questions.explanation: A is correct. Increased accidents (I) prompt authorities to tighten regulations → stricter drunk-driving penalties (II) as a response. I is cause; II is effect. The government acts BECAUSE accidents increased. Trap: II→I = increased penalties causing MORE accidents is counterintuitive (penalties are deterrents, not causes of accidents); 'independent' = ignores the clear policy-response logic.

questions.stem: Two statements: (I) The city received exceptionally heavy rainfall this monsoon. (II) Many low-lying areas of the city experienced severe flooding. Which is cause and which is effect?

options.option_text: I is cause; II is effect
II is cause; I is effect
Both are independent events
Both are effects of poor urban planning

questions.explanation: A is correct. Exceptionally heavy rainfall (I) → low-lying areas flood (II). Direct physical causation: water causes flooding. I is cause; II is effect. Trap: 'both effects of poor urban planning' = while poor drainage may contribute to flooding severity, the IMMEDIATE cause stated is heavy rainfall; the question asks about the relationship BETWEEN these two statements specifically.

questions.stem: Two statements: (I) The national cricket team performed poorly in the recent international tournament. (II) A new coach was appointed for the national cricket team. What is the relationship?

options.option_text: I is cause; II is effect
II is cause; I is effect
Both are independent
II is cause; I happened before II

questions.explanation: A is correct. Poor performance (I) typically triggers management decisions → appointment of a new coach (II). Sports boards respond to poor results by changing leadership. I is cause; II is effect. Trap: II→I = new coach's appointment causing poor performance is possible in theory (transition phase) but the MORE COMMON SSC logic is: poor results → change in coaching staff. Context determines the dominant causal direction.

questions.stem: Two statements: (I) The stock market index declined sharply today. (II) A major political party announced an alliance with another party today. Are these cause and effect?

options.option_text: I is cause; II is effect
II is cause; I is effect
Both I and II are independent events
Both are effects of the same cause

questions.explanation: C is correct. A political alliance announcement typically reflects positive stability (markets often react positively or neutrally to alliances). There is no clear causal link between a party alliance and a stock market DECLINE. These are most likely independent events happening on the same day. SSC rule: just because two events occur together doesn't mean one caused the other. Political alliance ≠ market decline without a specific stated mechanism. Trap: assuming any two events on the same day must be causally related.

questions.stem: Two statements: (I) The city's water supply authority has increased water tariffs by 30%. (II) The city has been facing a severe water shortage for the past three months. What is the relationship?

options.option_text: I is cause; II is effect
II is cause; I is effect
Both are independent
Both I and II are effects

questions.explanation: B is correct. Water shortage (II) → authority raises tariffs to reduce consumption and fund supply improvements (I). Shortage prompts a price response. II is cause; I is effect. Trap: I→II = raising tariffs caused the shortage? While demand reduction from higher prices could theoretically help, the passage implies shortage PRECEDED and CAUSED the tariff hike (standard regulatory response to scarcity).

questions.stem: Two statements: (I) Company X declared a 50% dividend for its shareholders this quarter. (II) Company X reported its highest-ever quarterly profit this quarter. What is the relationship?

options.option_text: I is cause; II is effect
II is cause; I is effect
Both are independent events
Both are effects of some other cause

questions.explanation: B is correct. Record profit (II) → company rewards shareholders with high dividend (I). Companies typically declare higher dividends when they have strong earnings. II is the financial cause; I is the resulting shareholder-return decision. Trap: I→II = declaring dividends caused profits? No — dividends are paid FROM profits, not a cause of profits; 'independent' = ignores the clear corporate finance relationship.

questions.stem: Two statements: (I) Three prominent professors left a well-known university this month. (II) The university announced significant cuts to research funding this month. What is the most likely relationship?

options.option_text: I is cause; II is effect
II is cause; I is effect
Both are independent events
I and II are effects of reduced student enrolment

questions.explanation: B is correct. Research funding cuts (II) → professors with research-dependent roles leave for better-funded institutions (I). Academic departures following funding cuts is a well-established pattern. II is cause; I is effect. Trap: I→II = professors leaving caused funding cuts? Possible but less likely — institutions usually cut funding for financial reasons, not because people left; they leave BECAUSE of cuts. 'Student enrolment' = a possible cause, but NOT stated in either statement (don't invent unstated causes in SSC reasoning).
